## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`

## Unauthorized and Forbidden responses¶ {#unauthorized-and-forbidden-responses}

When an unauthenticated request is denied permission there are two different error codes that may be appropriate.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.2)
HTTP 403 Permission Denied (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.4)

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header.

## How authentication is determined¶ {#how-authentication-is-determined}

The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
using the return value of the first class that successfully authenticates.

If no class authenticates,
`request.user`
will be set to an instance of
`django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser`
, and
`request.auth`
will be set to
`None`
.

The value of
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
for unauthenticated requests can be modified using the
`UNAUTHENTICATED_USER`
and
`UNAUTHENTICATED_TOKEN`
settings.

## Adding login to the Browsable API¶ {#adding-login-to-the-browsable-api}

If you open a browser and navigate to the browsable API at the moment, you'll find that you're no longer able to create new code snippets.  In order to do so we'd need to be able to login as a user.

We can add a login view for use with the browsable API, by editing the URLconf in our project-level
`urls.py`
file.

Add the following import at the top of the file:


`fromdjango.urlsimportpath,include`


And, at the end of the file, add a pattern to include the login and logout views for the browsable API.


`urlpatterns+=[path("api-auth/",include("rest_framework.urls")),]`


The
`'api-auth/'`
part of pattern can actually be whatever URL you want to use.

`permission_classes=[permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly,IsOwnerOrReadOnly]`


Make sure to also import the
`IsOwnerOrReadOnly`
class.


`fromsnippets.permissionsimportIsOwnerOrReadOnly`


Now, if you open a browser again, you find that the 'DELETE' and 'PUT' actions only appear on a snippet instance endpoint if you're logged in as the same user that created the code snippet.

### IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly¶ {#isauthenticatedorreadonly}

The
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
will allow authenticated users to perform any request.  Requests for unauthenticated users will only be permitted if the request method is one of the "safe" methods;
`GET`
,
`HEAD`
or
`OPTIONS`
.

This permission is suitable if you want to your API to allow read permissions to anonymous users, and only allow write permissions to authenticated users.

### DjangoModelPermissions¶ {#djangomodelpermissions}

## API Reference¶ {#api-reference}

### AllowAny¶ {#allowany}

The
`AllowAny`
permission class will allow unrestricted access,
regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated
.

This permission is not strictly required, since you can achieve the same result by using an empty list or tuple for the permissions setting, but you may find it useful to specify this class because it makes the intention explicit.

### IsAuthenticated¶ {#isauthenticated}

The
`IsAuthenticated`
permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to registered users.

### IsAdminUser¶ {#isadminuser}

The
`IsAdminUser`
permission class will deny permission to any user, unless
`user.is_staff`
is
`True`
in which case permission will be allowed.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to a subset of trusted administrators.

Permission checks are always run at the very start of the view, before any other code is allowed to proceed.  Permission checks will typically use the authentication information in the
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
properties to determine if the incoming request should be permitted.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

## How permissions are determined¶ {#how-permissions-are-determined}

Permissions in REST framework are always defined as a list of permission classes.

The default behavior can also be overridden to support custom model permissions.  For example, you might want to include a
`view`
model permission for
`GET`
requests.

To use custom model permissions, override
`DjangoModelPermissions`
and set the
`.perms_map`
property.  Refer to the source code for details.

### DjangoModelPermissionsOrAnonReadOnly¶ {#djangomodelpermissionsoranonreadonly}

Similar to
`DjangoModelPermissions`
, but also allows unauthenticated users to have read-only access to the API.

This permission class ties into Django's standard
object permissions framework (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/auth/customizing/#handling-object-permissions)
that allows per-object permissions on models.  In order to use this permission class, you'll also need to add a permission backend that supports object-level permissions, such as
django-guardian (https://github.com/lukaszb/django-guardian)
.

### DjangoModelPermissions¶ {#djangomodelpermissions}

This permission class ties into Django's standard
`django.contrib.auth`
model permissions (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/auth/customizing/#custom-permissions)
.  This permission must only be applied to views that have a
`.queryset`
property or
`get_queryset()`
method. Authorization will only be granted if the user
is authenticated
and has the
relevant model permissions
assigned. The appropriate model is determined by checking
`get_queryset().model`
or
`queryset.model`

`POST`

`add`
permission on the model.
`PUT`
and
`PATCH`
requests require the user to have the
`change`
permission on the model.
`DELETE`
requests require the user to have the

```python
    "PAGE_SIZE": 10,
}
```

```python
    "DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS": "rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination",
    "PAGE_SIZE": 100,
```

#### New pagination schemes.¶ {#new-pagination-schemes}

Until now, there has only been a single built-in pagination style in REST framework. We now have page, limit/offset and cursor based schemes included by default.

The cursor based pagination scheme is particularly smart, and is a better approach for clients iterating through large or frequently changing result sets. The scheme supports paging against non-unique indexes, by using both cursor and limit/offset information. It also allows for both forward and reverse cursor pagination. user_input: Once a list endpoint is paginated, what does the response body actually look like — how is a client supposed to know how many records exist in total and where to get the next batch?
reference: The results get wrapped in an envelope rather than returned as a bare array. A page-number paginated response carries `count` (the total number of records across all pages), `next` and `previous` (full URLs to the adjacent pages, or null at either end), and `results` (the records for this page). Clients walk the collection by following `next` until it comes back null, rather than by computing page numbers themselves.
reference_contexts: HTTP 200 OK { "count": 1023, "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5", "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3", "results": [ ... ] }
llm_response:
The structure of the response body depends on the pagination style configured:

*   **Default/Built-in Styles:** The built-in pagination styles include pagination links as part of the response body [7].
*   **Custom `Link` Header Style:** If configured to use a `Link` header (e.g., `LinkHeaderPagination`), the pagination links are moved out of the response body and into the `Link` header [1].
*   **Custom Response Body:** You can define a custom pagination class to structure the response body as desired. For example, by overriding `get_paginated_response`, you can nest links and include a total record count in the body:
    ```python
    return Response({
        'links': {
            'next': self.get_next_link(),
            'previous': self.get_previous_link()
        },
        'count': self.page.paginator.count,
        'results': data
    })
    ```

**How a client knows the total count and next batch:**
*   **Total records:** If the pagination class is configured to include it (as shown in the custom example above), the client retrieves the total count from a field like `'count'` in the response body [4].
*   **Next batch:** 
    *   If using the default built-in styles, the client finds the URL for the next batch within the response body [7].
    *   If using the `Link` header style, the client retrieves the URL for the next batch from the `Link` header [1].
    *   If using `CursorPagination`, the client uses an opaque "cursor" indicator to navigate to the next or previous set of results [2].

### Customizing the controls¶ {#customizing-the-controls}

### CursorPagination¶ {#cursorpagination}

The cursor-based pagination presents an opaque "cursor" indicator that the client may use to page through the result set. This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.

Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Cursor based pagination is more complex than other schemes. It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. However it does provide the following benefits:

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly
`CursorPagination`
ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
Supports usage with very large datasets. With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable. Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail. You'll need to think about what ordering you want the scheme to be applied against. The default is to order by
`"-created"`
. This assumes that
there must be a 'created' timestamp field
on the model instances, and will present a "timeline" style paginated view, with the most recently added items first.

—
Django documentation (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/pagination/)

reference: Add DRF's SearchFilter to the view and give it a search_fields attribute; the filter only activates once search_fields is set.

llm_response:
To enable clients to search your list endpoint with `?search=`, you must perform the following steps:

1.  **Add `SearchFilter` to the view:** Include `filters.SearchFilter` in the `filter_backends` attribute of your view.
2.  **Set `search_fields`:** Define a `search_fields` attribute on your view, which should be a list of the names of the text-type fields (e.g., `CharField` or `TextField`) on the model you wish to search.

**Example:**
```python
from rest_framework import filters, generics

class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.SearchFilter]
    search_fields = ['username', 'email']
```

By default, the query parameter is named `'search'`. If you need to change this name, you can override it using the `SEARCH_PARAM` setting in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` configuration.

This is the recommended approach to prevent unexpected data leakage, such as allowing users to order by sensitive fields like password hashes.

You can implement this by adding the `filters.OrderingFilter` to your view's `filter_backends` and defining the `ordering_fields` as a list of strings:

```python
    serializer_class = UserSerializer

```

reference: Yes — use the Meta option read_only_fields with a list/tuple of field names.

Yes, you can use the `read_only_fields` option in the `Meta` class as a shortcut to specify multiple read-only fields instead of adding `read_only=True` to each field individually.

```python
        fields = ['field1', 'field2', 'field3']
        read_only_fields = ['field1', 'field2']
```

Additionally, note that model fields with `editable=False` set and `AutoField` fields are set to read-only by default and do not need to be added to `read_only_fields`.

### Validation¶ {#validation}

#### Using.is_valid(raise_exception=True)¶ {#using-is_validraise_exceptiontrue}

The
`.is_valid()`
method now takes an optional boolean flag,
`raise_exception`
.

Calling
`.is_valid(raise_exception=True)`
will cause a
`ValidationError`
to be raised if the serializer data contains validation errors. This error will be handled by REST framework's default exception handler, allowing you to remove error response handling from your view code.

The handling and formatting of error responses may be altered globally by using the
`EXCEPTION_HANDLER`
settings key.

This change also means it's now possible to alter the style of error responses used by the built-in generic views, without having to include mixin classes or other overrides.

#### Usingserializers.ValidationError.¶ {#using-serializersvalidationerror}

Previously
`serializers.ValidationError`
error was simply a synonym for
`django.core.exceptions.ValidationError`
. This has now been altered so that it inherits from the standard
`APIException`
base class.

The reason behind this is that Django's
`ValidationError`
class is intended for use with HTML forms and its API makes using it slightly awkward with nested validation errors that can occur in serializers.

For most users this change shouldn't require any updates to your codebase, but it is worth ensuring that whenever raising validation errors you should prefer using the
`serializers.ValidationError`
exception class, and not Django's built-in exception.

We strongly recommend that you use the namespaced import style of
`import serializers`
and not
`from serializers import ValidationError`
in order to avoid any potential confusion.

user_input: What's a SerializerMethodField for?
reference: A read-only field whose value comes from a method on the serializer, letting you add arbitrary computed data to the output.
reference_contexts: This is a read-only field. It gets its value by calling a method on the serializer class it is attached to.
llm_response:
A `SerializerMethodField` is a read-only field used to add any sort of data to the serialized representation of an object. It retrieves its value by calling a method on the serializer class to which it is attached.

**How to use it:**
*   **Define the field:** Add it to your serializer class.
*   **Define the method:** By default, the field looks for a method named `get_<field_name>`. You can specify a different method name using the `method_name` argument in the `SerializerMethodField` signature.
*   **Method requirements:** The method must accept two arguments: `self` and the object being serialized. It should return the value you want included in the serialized output.

**Example:**
```python
class UserSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    days_since_joined = serializers.SerializerMethodField()

    class Meta:
        model = User
        fields = '__all__'

    def get_days_since_joined(self, obj):
        return (now() - obj.date_joined).days
```

`method_name`

The serializer method referred to by the
`method_name`

`self`

Each serializer field class constructor takes at least these arguments.  Some Field classes take additional, field-specific arguments, but the following should always be accepted:

### read_only¶ {#read_only}

Read-only fields are included in the API output, but should not be included in the input during create or update operations. Any 'read_only' fields that are incorrectly included in the serializer input will be ignored.

Set this to
`True`

`False`

### write_only¶ {#write_only}

Set this to
`True`
to ensure that the field may be used when updating or creating an instance, but is not included when serializing the representation.

Defaults to

### required¶ {#required}

Model fields which have
`editable=False`
set, and
`AutoField`
fields will be set to read-only by default, and do not need to be added to the
`read_only_fields`
option.

Note
There is a special-case where a read-only field is part of a
`unique_together`
constraint at the model level. In this case the field is required by the serializer class in order to validate the constraint, but should also not be editable by the user.
The right way to deal with this is to specify the field explicitly on the serializer, providing both the
`read_only=True`
and
`default=…`
keyword arguments.
One example of this is a read-only relation to the currently authenticated
`User`
which is
`unique_together`
with another identifier. In this case you would declare the user field like so:

`user=serializers.PrimaryKeyRelatedField(read_only=True,default=serializers.CurrentUserDefault())`

user_input: How does the source argument on a serializer field work?
reference: source names the attribute used to populate the field; it can be a no-arg method or a dotted path like 'user.email' to traverse relations.
reference_contexts: The name of the attribute that will be used to populate the field.
llm_response:
The `source` argument controls which attribute is used to populate a serializer field and can point to any attribute on the serialized instance. It defaults to the name of the field.

### Usage and Functionality
*   **Attribute Traversal:** You can use dotted notation (e.g., `source="user.email"`) to traverse attributes in a manner similar to Django's template language.
*   **Passing the Entire Object:** Using `source='*'` indicates that the entire object should be passed to the field. This is useful for nested representations or when a field requires access to the complete object to determine its output. When using `source='*'`, `to_internal_value` maps back to a dictionary that updates the root validated data dictionary rather than a single key.

### Considerations
*   **Performance:** When using dotted notation to access relational ORM models, be aware of potential N+1 problems. If the related objects are not prefetched, they will be fetched from the database. It is recommended to use `prefetch_related` and `select_related` to avoid this.
*   **Missing Data:** When using dotted notation, you may need to provide a `default` value if an object is empty or not present during attribute traversal.

#### serializer_field_mapping¶ {#serializer_field_mapping}

Dealing with relationships between entities is one of the more challenging aspects of Web API design.  There are a number of different ways that we might choose to represent a relationship:

Using primary keys.
Using hyperlinking between entities.
Using a unique identifying slug field on the related entity.
Using the default string representation of the related entity.
Nesting the related entity inside the parent representation.
Some other custom representation.

## Custom relational fields¶ {#custom-relational-fields}

In rare cases where none of the existing relational styles fit the representation you need,

To implement a custom relational field, you should override

user_input: In tests, how do I authenticate a request without the real credential flow?
reference: Use force_authenticate() to directly authenticate the request against a user (and optionally a token).
reference_contexts: To forcibly authenticate a request, use the force_authenticate() method.
llm_response:
To authenticate a request in tests without the real credential flow, you can use the `force_authenticate()` method.

### When using `APIRequestFactory`
When testing views directly with `APIRequestFactory`, use the `force_authenticate()` function. This allows you to authenticate a request without constructing the actual credentials.

**Usage:**
```python
from rest_framework.test import force_authenticate, APIRequestFactory

factory = APIRequestFactory()
user = User.objects.get(username='olivia')
request = factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')

# You can set the user, the token, or both
force_authenticate(request, user=user, token=user.auth_token)
```

### When using `APIClient`
If you are using `APIClient`, it also provides a `.force_authenticate()` method that functions similarly to the standalone function.

**Usage:**
```python
client = APIClient()
client.force_authenticate(user=user, token=token)
```

### Alternative: Setting Headers
If you prefer to test the authentication headers directly (such as for Basic, OAuth1a, or OAuth2 authentication), you can use the `.credentials()` method on an `APIClient` instance. This sets headers to be included on all subsequent requests.

**Usage:**
```python
client = APIClient()
client.credentials(HTTP_AUTHORIZATION='Token ' + token.key)
```
*Note: Calling `.credentials()` a second time overwrites existing credentials. Calling it with no arguments unsets all credentials.*

## RequestsClient¶ {#requestsclient}

REST framework also includes a client for interacting with your application
using the popular Python library,
`requests`
. This may be useful if:

You are expecting to interface with the API primarily from another Python service,
and want to test the service at the same level as the client will see.
You want to write tests in such a way that they can also be run against a staging or
live environment. (See "Live tests" below.)

This exposes exactly the same interface as if you were using a requests session
directly.


`fromrest_framework.testimportRequestsClientclient=RequestsClient()response=client.get('http://testserver/users/')assertresponse.status_code==200`

Note that
`RequestsClient`
mounts a WSGI adapter and does not perform real
network I/O. It cannot be used to send HTTP requests to remote services such
as staging or production servers. For live tests against a deployed service,
you should instead use a plain
`requests.Session`
(or similar HTTP client)
configured with the appropriate base URL and authentication.
Using this style to create basic tests of a few core pieces of functionality is
a powerful way to validate your live service. Doing so may require some careful
attention to setup and teardown to ensure that the tests run in a way that they
do not directly affect customer data.

The

The client may also specify reverse orderings by prefixing the field name with '-', like so:


`http://example.com/api/users?ordering=-username`


Multiple orderings may also be specified:

## Request objects¶ {#request-objects}

#### The.dataand.query_paramsproperties.¶ {#the-data-and-query_params-properties}

The usage of
`request.DATA`
and
`request.FILES`
is now pending deprecation in favor of a single
`request.data`
attribute that contains
all
the parsed data.

Having separate attributes is reasonable for web applications that only ever parse url-encoded or multipart requests, but makes less sense for the general-purpose request parsing that REST framework supports.

You may now pass all the request data to a serializer class in a single argument:


`# Do this...ExampleSerializer(data=request.data)`


Instead of passing the files argument separately:


`# Don't do this...ExampleSerializer(data=request.DATA,files=request.FILES)`


The usage of
`request.QUERY_PARAMS`
is now pending deprecation in favor of the lowercased
`request.query_params`
.

### Thequerysetargument¶ {#the-queryset-argument}

The
`queryset`
argument is only ever required for
writable
relationship field, in which case it is used for performing the model instance lookup, that maps from the primitive user input, into a model instance.

In version 2.x a serializer class could
sometimes

if

`ModelSerializer`

This behavior is now replaced with
always

`queryset`
argument for writable relational fields.

reference: rest_framework.reverse.reverse behaves like django.urls.reverse but returns a fully qualified URL using the request's host/port — so pass the request.
reference_contexts: Signature: reverse(viewname, *args, **kwargs) Has the same behavior as django.urls.reverse , except that it returns a fully qualified URL, using the request to determine the host and port.
llm_response:
DRF's `reverse()` is a utility function that provides the same behavior as `django.urls.reverse`, with two key differences:

*   **Fully qualified URLs:** It returns a fully qualified URL by using the `request` to determine the host and port.
*   **Versioning support:** It ties into the API's versioning scheme. By including the current `request` as a keyword argument, the function applies URL transformations appropriate to the request version (e.g., prepending a version prefix or adding a version query parameter).

To use these features, you must include the `request` as a keyword argument:

```python
from rest_framework.reverse import reverse
reverse('view-name', request=request)
```

`request`
as a keyword argument, like so.

The above function will apply any URL transformations appropriate to the request version. For example:

If
`NamespaceVersioning`
was being used, and the API version was 'v1', then the URL lookup used would be
`'v1:bookings-list'`

If
`QueryParameterVersioning`
was being used, and the API version was

# Versioning¶ {#versioning}

Versioning an interface is just a "polite" way to kill deployed clients.
—
Roy Fielding (https://www.slideshare.net/evolve_conference/201308-fielding-evolve/31)
.

API versioning allows you to alter behavior between different clients. REST framework provides for a number of different versioning schemes.

Versioning is determined by the incoming client request, and may either be based on the request URL, or based on the request headers.

There are a number of valid approaches to approaching versioning.
Non-versioned systems can also be appropriate (https://www.infoq.com/articles/roy-fielding-on-versioning)
, particularly if you're engineering for very long-term systems with multiple clients outside of your control.

## Versioning with REST framework¶ {#versioning-with-rest-framework}

user_input: What does @api_view do to a plain function view?
reference: It wraps the function so it gets a DRF Request and returns a DRF Response for the listed HTTP methods; by default only GET is accepted and others get a 405.
reference_contexts: By default only GET methods will be accepted. Other methods will respond with "405 Method Not Allowed".
llm_response:
The `@api_view` decorator wraps a function-based view to provide the following functionality:

*   **Request/Response Handling:** It ensures the view receives `Request` instances and adds context to `Response` objects to enable content negotiation.
*   **Method Handling:** It restricts the view to specific HTTP methods. By default, only `GET` is accepted; other methods return a "405 Method Not Allowed" response. You can specify allowed methods by passing a list to the decorator (e.g., `@api_view(['GET', 'POST'])`).
*   **Error Handling:** It handles `ParseError` exceptions that occur when accessing `request.data` with malformed input.
*   **Configuration:** It ensures the view uses the default renderers, parsers, and authentication classes specified in the settings, and it automatically sets the `parsers` property based on the `parser_classes` or `DEFAULT_PARSER_CLASSES` setting.

reference_contexts: Token authentication is appropriate for client-server setups, such as native desktop and mobile clients.
REST framework provides a built-in view to provide this behavior.

The obtain_auth_token view will return a JSON response when valid username and password fields are POSTed to the view using form data or JSON: { 'token' : '9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b' } Note that the default obtain_auth_token view explicitly uses JSON requests and responses, rather than using default renderer and parser classes in your settings.

The DRF-native approach for token-based authentication in mobile clients is `TokenAuthentication`.

### Implementation and Requirements
*   **Installation/Migration:** You must ensure `rest_framework.authtoken` is included in your `INSTALLED_APPS` and run migrations to create the necessary database tables for storing tokens.
*   **Generating Tokens:** You can create tokens for users programmatically using `rest_framework.authtoken.models.Token.objects.create(user=...)` or via the management command `drf_create_token`.

To allow everyone to browse data while restricting modification or deletion to the record creator, you should implement a custom permission class by overriding `BasePermission` and implementing the `.has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj)` method.

### Implementation Steps:

1.  **Custom Permission:** Create a class that inherits from `BasePermission`. In the `.has_object_permission` method, check if the request method is a "safe" method (e.g., `GET`, `HEAD`, or `OPTIONS`). If it is, return `True` to allow browsing. For other methods (like `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`), check if `obj.owner == request.user` (or the equivalent field representing the creator) and return `True` only if they match.
2.  **View Configuration:** Apply this custom permission class to your views via the `permission_classes` attribute.
3.  **Queryset Filtering:** Because generic views do not automatically apply object-level permissions to each instance in a list, you should filter the `queryset` or `get_queryset()` method to ensure users only see what they are permitted to view. You can achieve this by overriding `get_queryset()` on your views or by using a filter backend.

### Alternative Approaches:
*   **DjangoObjectPermissions:** You can use `DjangoObjectPermissions`, which requires the user to have relevant model and object-level permissions. This does not require the `django-guardian` package but supports object-level backends.
*   **DjangoObjectPermissionsFilter:** If you use `django-guardian` for your object-level permissions backend, you can use the `DjangoObjectPermissionsFilter` class from the `djangorestframework-guardian` package to ensure list endpoints only return objects for which the user has appropriate view permissions.

Note that object-level permissions from `has_object_permission()` are not applied when creating objects because `get_object()` is not called. To restrict object creation, you must implement the check in your Serializer class or override the `perform_create()` method in your ViewSet.

llm_response:
To associate a record with the logged-in user without the client sending the owner field, follow these steps:

1.  **Override `.perform_create()` in your view:**
    The user is a property of the incoming request rather than the serialized representation. Override the `.perform_create()` method in your view class to pass the user to the serializer's save method:
    ```python
    def perform_create(self, serializer):
        serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
    ```
    This ensures the `create()` method of the serializer receives the `'owner'` field along with the validated data from the request.

2.  **Update your serializer:**
    To ensure the field is read-only (so the client cannot modify it) and to reflect the association in your API output, add the following field to your serializer definition:
    ```python
    owner = serializers.ReadOnlyField(source="owner.username")
    ```
    Ensure you also include `'owner'` in the `fields` list of your serializer's inner `Meta` class.

llm_response:
To cap requests for anonymous and logged-in users, you should use `AnonRateThrottle` and `UserRateThrottle` respectively. You can apply both simultaneously to impose different constraints on these groups.

### Mechanism
*   **`AnonRateThrottle`**: Used to restrict unauthenticated users based on their IP address.
*   **`UserRateThrottle`**: Used to restrict authenticated users based on their user ID. If a request is unauthenticated, it falls back to using the IP address.

### Where to set the numbers
The allowed request rates are determined by the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES` setting in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` configuration. You define the rates using the keys `'anon'` and `'user'`.

**Example configuration:**
```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle',
        'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle'
    ],
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {
        'anon': '100/day',
        'user': '1000/day'
    }
}
```

**Alternative approach:**
You can also override the `rate` property directly on a subclass of `AnonRateThrottle` or `UserRateThrottle` and set that property to your desired value. This takes precedence over the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES` setting.

The

## Custom throttles¶ {#custom-throttles}

To create a custom throttle, override
`BaseThrottle`
and implement
`.allow_request(self, request, view)`
.  The method should return
`True`
if the request should be allowed, and
`False`
otherwise.

Optionally you may also override the
`.wait()`
method.  If implemented,
`.wait()`
should return a recommended number of seconds to wait before attempting the next request, or
`None`
.  The
`.wait()`
method will only be called if
`.allow_request()`
has previously returned
`False`
.

`UserRateThrottle`
is suitable if you want simple global rate restrictions per-user.

### ScopedRateThrottle¶ {#scopedratethrottle}

The
`ScopedRateThrottle`
class can be used to restrict access to specific parts of the API.  This throttle will only be applied if the view that is being accessed includes a
`.throttle_scope`
property.  The unique throttle key will then be formed by concatenating the "scope" of the request with the unique user id or IP address.

The allowed request rate is determined by the
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
setting using a key from the request "scope".

For example, given the following views...


`classContactListView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classContactDetailView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classUploadView(APIView):throttle_scope='uploads'...`


...and the following settings.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

## A note on concurrency¶ {#a-note-on-concurrency}

The built-in throttle implementations are open to
race conditions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_condition#Data_race)
, so under high concurrency they may allow a few extra requests through.

If your project relies on guaranteeing the number of requests during concurrent requests, you will need to implement your own throttle class. See
issue #5181 (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/issues/5181)
for more details.

Throttling is similar to
permissions (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
, in that it determines if a request should be authorized.  Throttles indicate a temporary state, and are used to control the rate of requests that clients can make to an API.

As with permissions, multiple throttles may be used.  Your API might have a restrictive throttle for unauthenticated requests, and a less restrictive throttle for authenticated requests.

Another scenario where you might want to use multiple throttles would be if you need to impose different constraints on different parts of the API, due to some services being particularly resource-intensive.

user_input: Scrapers hit us in short violent bursts; our real users trickle requests out over the whole day. If I set the ceiling low enough to stop a burst I punish the real users, and if I set it high enough for the real users the bursts sail through. Can I enforce both shapes at once?
reference: Yes — stack two throttles instead of picking one number. Subclass UserRateThrottle twice and give each subclass its own unique `scope`, e.g. a `burst` class and a `sustained` class, then list both in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES and define a rate for each scope under DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES (something like '60/min' and '1000/day'). Multiple UserRateThrottles can be in force at the same time, and every request is checked against all of them, so a client has to stay under the short window and the long one simultaneously.

llm_response:
Yes, you can enforce both burst and sustained rates at the same time by using multiple throttles.

To implement this, you should override `UserRateThrottle` to create separate classes for each rate, assigning each a unique `scope`. You then include these classes in your `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` setting and define the corresponding rates in `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`.

**Example implementation:**

1. Define the custom throttle classes:
```python
class BurstRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle):
    scope = 'burst'

class SustainedRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle):
    scope = 'sustained'
```

2. Configure the settings:
```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES': [
        'example.throttles.BurstRateThrottle',
        'example.throttles.SustainedRateThrottle'
    ],
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {
        'burst': '60/min',
        'sustained': '1000/day'
    }
}
```

The rates in `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES` can be specified using periods of second, minute, hour, or day (e.g., `s`, `m`, `h`, `d`).

### ScopedRateThrottle¶ {#scopedratethrottle}

The
`ScopedRateThrottle`
class can be used to restrict access to specific parts of the API.  This throttle will only be applied if the view that is being accessed includes a
`.throttle_scope`
property.  The unique throttle key will then be formed by concatenating the "scope" of the request with the unique user id or IP address.

The allowed request rate is determined by the
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
setting using a key from the request "scope".

For example, given the following views...


`classContactListView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classContactDetailView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classUploadView(APIView):throttle_scope='uploads'...`


...and the following settings.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`

...and the following settings.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`


User requests to either
`ContactListView`
or
`ContactDetailView`
would be restricted to a total of 1000 requests per-day.  User requests to
`UploadView`

The

will throttle users to a given rate of requests across the API.  The user id is used to generate a unique key to throttle against.  Unauthenticated requests will fall back to using the IP address of the incoming request to generate a unique key to throttle against.

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

## How clients are identified¶ {#how-clients-are-identified}

The
`X-Forwarded-For`
HTTP header and

`REMOTE_ADDR`
variable from the WSGI environment will be used.

I want it to answer with a clean, machine-readable 'try again shortly' that our clients can branch on, and I want to define that once rather than writing the same try/except into every view that touches the provider.
reference: Define your own exception type and raise it; the framework turns it into the response. Subclass APIException — the base class for exceptions raised inside an APIView or @api_view — and set `.status_code`, `.default_detail` and `.default_code` on the class, e.g. a ServiceUnavailable with status_code = 503 and a default_detail of 'Service temporarily unavailable, try again later.'. Then any view that raises it produces that response, handled centrally instead of per view, and the body comes back in the standard error shape with a `detail` key rather than as a Django HTML error page. Note the boundary: this handling only applies to responses generated by *raised* exceptions — a Response object you return directly from a view, such as an explicit HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST, never passes through it.

The web client needs the full object from the same endpoint. I'd rather not stand up a parallel serializer and a parallel URL just to serve a narrower version of the same record.
reference: You don't need a second serializer class — the field set is mutable at runtime. Once a serializer is initialized its fields are available as the `.fields` attribute, an ordinary dictionary you can read and modify, which lets you change what gets rendered (and the arguments on individual fields) per instance rather than at declaration time. The documented pattern is a DynamicFieldsModelSerializer: accept an extra `fields` keyword in __init__, pop it before calling super(), and then drop everything not requested from self.fields. Your view decides what to pass — typically driven by a query parameter — so UserSerializer(user) returns the full record and UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email')) returns the narrow one from the same class and the same URL. If you'd rather not hand-roll it, drf-dynamic-fields provides a mixin that limits fields from a URL parameter, and drf-flex-fields additionally handles expanding primitive fields into nested ones.
reference_contexts: Once a serializer has been initialized, the dictionary of fields that are set on the serializer may be accessed using the .fields attribute. Accessing and modifying this attribute allows you to dynamically modify the serializer.
Modifying the fields argument directly allows you to do interesting things such as changing the arguments on serializer fields at runtime, rather than at the point of declaring the serializer.

class DynamicFieldsModelSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer): """ A ModelSerializer that takes an additional `fields` argument that controls which fields should be displayed. """ def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): # Don't pass the 'fields' arg up to the superclass fields = kwargs.pop('fields', None) # Instantiate the superclass normally super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
print(UserSerializer(user)) {'id': 2, 'username': 'jonwatts', 'email': 'jon@example.com'} print(UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email'))) {'id': 2, 'email': 'jon@example.com'}
The drf-dynamic-fields package provides a mixin to dynamically limit the fields per serializer to a subset specified by an URL parameter.

### Customizing multiple update¶ {#customizing-multiple-update}

By default the
`ListSerializer`
class does not support multiple updates. This is because the behavior that should be expected for insertions and deletions is ambiguous.

To support multiple updates you'll need to do so explicitly. When writing your multiple update code make sure to keep the following in mind:

How do you determine which instance should be updated for each item in the list of data?
How should insertions be handled? Are they invalid, or do they create new objects?
How should removals be handled? Do they imply object deletion, or removing a relationship? Should they be silently ignored, or are they invalid?
How should ordering be handled? Does changing the position of two items imply any state change or is it ignored?

#### The.dataand.query_paramsproperties.¶ {#the-data-and-query_params-properties}

The usage of
`request.DATA`
and
`request.FILES`
is now pending deprecation in favor of a single
`request.data`
attribute that contains
all
the parsed data.

Having separate attributes is reasonable for web applications that only ever parse url-encoded or multipart requests, but makes less sense for the general-purpose request parsing that REST framework supports.

You may now pass all the request data to a serializer class in a single argument:


`# Do this...ExampleSerializer(data=request.data)`


Instead of passing the files argument separately:


`# Don't do this...ExampleSerializer(data=request.DATA,files=request.FILES)`


The usage of
`request.QUERY_PARAMS`
is now pending deprecation in favor of the lowercased
`request.query_params`
.

llm_response:
To set up a self-describing, browsable API that uses JSON as the primary format, follow these steps:

*   **Browsability:** The API is browsable by default. When requested by a web browser, the API automatically returns an HTML-formatted representation of the resource instead of JSON [7].
*   **Accessing JSON:** To view the raw JSON response in a browser, append `?format=json` to the URL [6]. You can also use the `URL_FORMAT_OVERRIDE` setting to control the `?format=` style URL parameters [2].
*   **Clickable URLs:** To make URLs in your resource output clickable for humans, include fully-qualified URLs in your resource output. The `rest_framework` package provides a `reverse` helper for this purpose [6].
*   **Authentication:** To add authentication to the browsable API, add the following routes to your `urlconf` [1]:
    ```python
    from django.urls import include, path
    ```

To address the performance issue with the browsable API form while keeping the UI enabled, you have the following options:

**1. Replace the select input with a text input (Recommended)**
The documentation identifies this as the "simplest option" for handling fields with a large number of items. You can replace the select widget with a standard text input by setting the `style` argument on the field:

```python
author = serializers.HyperlinkedRelatedField(
    queryset=User.objects.all(), 
    style={'base_template': 'input.html'}
)
```

**2. Rely on automatic select field cutoffs**
The browsable API has a built-in mechanism to prevent performance issues when rendering relational fields. By default, it will only display a maximum of 1000 selectable items. If your lookup table exceeds this, the system automatically displays a disabled option stating "More than 1000 items…". 

**3. Advanced Customization**
If you require further control, you can:
*   **Override `BrowsableAPIRenderer.get_context()`**: This allows you to customize the context passed to the template.
*   **Customize the template**: You can choose not to have `api.html` extend `base.html`, allowing you to define the page content and capabilities entirely yourself.

To version the behavior of a view in Django REST framework, you must first enable a versioning scheme.

### 1. Enable Versioning
You can enable versioning globally by setting the `DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS` in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS': 'rest_framework.versioning.NamespaceVersioning'
}
```

Alternatively, you can set the `versioning_class` on a per-view or per-viewset basis. You can also define custom versioning classes by subclassing existing schemes and setting `default_version`, `allowed_versions`, and `version_param`.

### 2. Vary Behavior Based on Version
Once enabled, the `request.version` attribute will contain the version string from the incoming request. You can use this attribute to switch logic within your view. A common approach is to override `get_serializer_class` to return different serializers based on the version:

```python
def get_serializer_class(self):
    if self.request.version == 'v1':
        return AccountSerializerVersion1
    return AccountSerializer
```

### 3. Additional Considerations
*   **URL Reversing:** When using URL-based versioning, use the `reverse` function provided by REST framework and pass the `request` as a keyword argument to ensure generated URLs include the correct version.
*   **Hyperlinked Serializers:** If using hyperlinked serialization with a URL-based versioning scheme, you must pass the `request` as context to the serializer:
    ```python
    serializer = BookingsSerializer(queryset, many=True, context={'request': request})
    ```
*   **Versioning Schemes:** REST framework supports several schemes, including URL-based (e.g., `NamespaceVersioning`, `URLPathVersioning`) and `Accept` header-based (`AcceptHeaderVersioning`).

# Versioning¶ {#versioning}

Versioning an interface is just a "polite" way to kill deployed clients.
—
Roy Fielding (https://www.slideshare.net/evolve_conference/201308-fielding-evolve/31)
.

API versioning allows you to alter behavior between different clients. REST framework provides for a number of different versioning schemes.

Versioning is determined by the incoming client request, and may either be based on the request URL, or based on the request headers.

There are a number of valid approaches to approaching versioning.
Non-versioned systems can also be appropriate (https://www.infoq.com/articles/roy-fielding-on-versioning)
, particularly if you're engineering for very long-term systems with multiple clients outside of your control.

When using hyperlinked serialization styles together with a URL based versioning scheme make sure to include the request as context to the serializer.

`DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS`
settings key.

Unless it is explicitly set, the value for
`DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS`
will be
`None`
. In this case the
`request.version`
attribute will always return
`None`

## Versioning with REST framework¶ {#versioning-with-rest-framework}

When API versioning is enabled, the
`request.version`
attribute will contain a string that corresponds to the version requested in the incoming client request.

By default, versioning is not enabled, and
`request.version`
will always return
`None`
.

### Varying behavior based on the version¶ {#varying-behavior-based-on-the-version}

How you vary the API behavior is up to you, but one example you might typically want is to switch to a different serialization style in a newer version. For example:


`defget_serializer_class(self):ifself.request.version=='v1':returnAccountSerializerVersion1returnAccountSerializer`


### Reversing URLs for versioned APIs¶ {#reversing-urls-for-versioned-apis}

The
`reverse`
function included by REST framework ties in with the versioning scheme. You need to make sure to include the current
`request`
as a keyword argument, like so.

You can also set your versioning class plus those three values on a per-view or a per-viewset basis by defining your own versioning scheme and using the
`default_version`
,
`allowed_versions`
and
`version_param`
class variables. For example, if you want to use
`URLPathVersioning`
:


`fromrest_framework.versioningimportURLPathVersioningfromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleVersioning(URLPathVersioning):default_version=...allowed_versions=...version_param=...classExampleView(APIVIew):versioning_class=ExampleVersioning`


## API Reference¶ {#api-reference}

### AcceptHeaderVersioning¶ {#acceptheaderversioning}

This scheme requires the client to specify the version as part of the media type in the
`Accept`
header. The version is included as a media type parameter, that supplements the main media type.

Here's an example HTTP request using the accept header versioning style.


`GET/bookings/HTTP/1.1Host:example.comAccept:application/json;version=1.0`

### Other versioning settings¶ {#other-versioning-settings}

The following settings keys are also used to control versioning:

`DEFAULT_VERSION`
. The value that should be used for
`request.version`
when no versioning information is present. Defaults to
`None`
.
`ALLOWED_VERSIONS`
. If set, this value will restrict the set of versions that may be returned by the versioning scheme, and will raise an error if the provided version is not in this set. Note that the value used for the
`DEFAULT_VERSION`
setting is always considered to be part of the
`ALLOWED_VERSIONS`
set (unless it is
`None`
). Defaults to
`None`
.
`VERSION_PARAM`
. The string that should be used for any versioning parameters, such as in the media type or URL query parameters. Defaults to
`'version'`
.

user_input: I want to expose an extra custom action on a viewset — like a 'highlight' endpoint on a snippet — that the router routes for me. How?
reference: Mark the method with @action and set detail=True or detail=False to say whether it acts on a single object or the collection; the router then builds its URL.
reference_contexts: If you have ad-hoc methods that should be routable, you can mark them as such with the @action decorator.
To indicate this, set the detail argument to True or False .
Use the url_path and url_name parameters to change the URL segment and the reverse URL name of the action.
REST framework adds support for automatic URL routing to Django, and provides you with a simple, quick and consistent way of wiring your view logic to a set of URLs.
llm_response:
To expose a custom action like `highlight` on a viewset so that the router handles it, use the `@action` decorator on the method within your viewset.

1.  **Define the method:** Decorate your method with `@action`. You must set the `detail` argument to `True` (if the action is for a single object) or `False` (if it is for the entire collection).
    *   Example: `@action(detail=True) def highlight(self, request, pk=None): ...`
2.  **Register with a router:** Do not use `.as_view()` for these methods, as it bypasses router setup. Instead, register your viewset with a router (such as `DefaultRouter`) in your `urls.py`:
    ```python
    from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
    router = DefaultRouter()
    router.register(r'snippets', SnippetViewSet, basename='snippet')
    urlpatterns = router.urls
    ```

**Additional configuration options:**
*   **HTTP Methods:** By default, custom actions respond to `GET` requests. Use the `methods` argument to change this (e.g., `methods=['post']`).
*   **URL Construction:** By default, the URL is based on the method name. To change the URL segment, use the `url_path` argument. To change the reverse URL name, use the `url_name` argument.
*   **Multiple Methods:** You can map additional HTTP methods to the same action using the `.mapping` attribute on the decorated method (e.g., `@highlight.mapping.delete`).

/

Custom actions which use the

The URLs for custom actions by default depend on the method name itself. If you want to change the way url should be constructed, you can include

user_input: Our front-end is deployed on a completely different domain from the API. The browser fires off an OPTIONS request and then refuses to send the real one, and none of this ever reaches our view code — no log line, nothing. What's the supported way to let this through?
reference: That's a cross-origin problem, not an authentication one: the browser is refusing to hand the response to a client on another domain unless the server returns headers permitting it. DRF's recommendation is to add those headers in middleware rather than in your views, so CORS is supported transparently across the whole API without changing view behaviour. The docs point at Adam Johnson's `django-cors-headers` package, which is known to work correctly with REST framework.
reference_contexts: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a mechanism for allowing clients to interact with APIs that are hosted on a different domain. CORS works by requiring the server to include a specific set of headers that allow a browser to determine if and when cross-domain requests should be allowed.

The best way to deal with CORS in REST framework is to add the required response headers in middleware. This ensures that CORS is supported transparently, without having to change any behavior in your views.
Adam Johnson maintains the django-cors-headers package, which is known to work correctly with REST framework APIs.
llm_response:
The supported way to handle cross-domain AJAX requests is to use CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing). The documentation explicitly recommends using CORS as the modern approach for cross-domain requests rather than using JSONP.

For details on implementing this, you should refer to the CORS documentation provided at: https://www.django-rest-framework.org/topics/ajax-csrf-cors/

## The hypermedia approach¶ {#the-hypermedia-approach}

To be fully RESTful an API should present its available actions as hypermedia controls in the responses that it sends.

In this approach, rather than documenting the available API endpoints up front, the description instead concentrates on the
media types
that are used.  The available actions that may be taken on any given URL are not strictly fixed, but are instead made available by the presence of link and form controls in the returned document.

To implement a hypermedia API you'll need to decide on an appropriate media type for the API, and implement a custom renderer and parser for that media type.  The
REST, Hypermedia & HATEOAS (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/topics/rest-hypermedia-hateoas/)
section of the documentation includes pointers to background reading, as well as links to various hypermedia formats.

## Self describing APIs¶ {#self-describing-apis}

The browsable API that REST framework provides makes it possible for your API to be entirely self describing.  The documentation for each API endpoint can be provided simply by visiting the URL in your browser.

#### Setting the title¶ {#setting-the-title}

The title that is used in the browsable API is generated from the view class name or function name.  Any trailing
`View`
or
`ViewSet`
suffix is stripped, and the string is whitespace separated on uppercase/lowercase boundaries or underscores.

For example, the view
`UserListView`
, will be named
`User List`
when presented in the browsable API.

When working with viewsets, an appropriate suffix is appended to each generated view.  For example, the view set
`UserViewSet`
will generate views named
`User List`
and
`User Instance`
.

#### Setting the description¶ {#setting-the-description}

The description in the browsable API is generated from the docstring of the view or viewset.

If the python
`Markdown`
library is installed, then
markdown syntax (https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/syntax)
may be used in the docstring, and will be converted to HTML in the browsable API.  For example:

This change means that you can now easily customize the style of error responses across your entire API, without having to modify any of the generic views.

## The metadata API¶ {#the-metadata-api}

Behavior for dealing with
`OPTIONS`
requests was previously built directly into the class-based views. This has now been properly separated out into a Metadata API that allows the same pluggable style as other API policies in REST framework.

This makes it far easier to use a different style for
`OPTIONS`
responses throughout your API, and makes it possible to create third-party metadata policies.

## Serializers as HTML forms¶ {#serializers-as-html-forms}

REST framework 3.0 includes templated HTML form rendering for serializers.

This API should not yet be considered finalized, and will only be promoted to public API for the 3.1 release.

Significant changes that you do need to be aware of include:

or

user_input: I want some endpoints to render as real HTML pages using my own templates. What renderer supports that and what does the view return?
reference: TemplateHTMLRenderer: the view returns a dict of context data and names a template, and the renderer builds the HTML page — serializers can even act as HTML forms in those templates.
reference_contexts: The TemplateHTMLRenderer class expects the response to contain a dictionary of context data, and renders an HTML page based on a template that must be specified either in the view or on the response.
Additionally, serializers can be used as HTML forms and rendered in templates.
REST framework is suitable for returning both API style responses, and regular HTML pages.
Renders data to HTML, using Django's standard template rendering.
llm_response:
To render real HTML pages using your own templates, you should use the `TemplateHTMLRenderer`.

### How it works:
*   **The Renderer:** You must set `renderer_classes` to `[TemplateHTMLRenderer]` in your view and specify a `template_name`.
*   **The View Return:** The view should return a `Response` object containing a dictionary of context data.

**Example:**
```python
from rest_framework.renderers import TemplateHTMLRenderer
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework.views import APIView

class ProfileList(APIView):
    renderer_classes = [TemplateHTMLRenderer]
    template_name = 'profile_list.html'

    def get(self, request):
        queryset = Profile.objects.all()
        return Response({'profiles': queryset})
```

### Alternative:
You can also use `StaticHTMLRenderer` if you want to return pre-rendered HTML. In this case, the view must return a `Response` object containing a string of the pre-rendered HTML content rather than a dictionary.

Before a TemplateResponse instance can be returned to the client, it must be rendered. The rendering process takes the intermediate representation of template and context, and turns it into the final byte stream that can be served to the client.

REST framework includes a number of built in Renderer classes, that allow you to return responses with various media types.  There is also support for defining your own custom renderers, which gives you the flexibility to design your own media types.

The method should return a bytestring, which will be used as the body of the HTTP response.

`Accept:`

attribute, and may include media type parameters.  For example
`"application/json; nested=true"`
.
`renderer_context=None`

`view`

`response`

`args`
,
`kwargs`
.

user_input: I want to accept a raw file upload from a native client streaming the file body, not a multipart form. How do I set up the parser and how does DRF get the filename?
reference: Use FileUploadParser, which puts the file at request.data['file']; the filename comes from a filename URL kwarg if present, otherwise the client sets it in Content-Disposition.
reference_contexts: The request.data property will be a dictionary with a single key 'file' containing the uploaded file.
If it is called without a filename URL keyword argument, then the client must set the filename in the Content-Disposition HTTP header.
.media_type : */* Note The FileUploadParser is for usage with native clients that can upload the file as a raw data request.
A list or tuple of parser classes, that determines the default set of parsers used when accessing the request.data property.
llm_response:
To accept a raw file upload from a native client, you must use the `FileUploadParser`.

### Setting up the parser
Because `FileUploadParser` has a `media_type` of `*/*`, it should generally be the only parser set on your API view. You configure it by setting the `parser_classes` attribute on your view:

```python
from rest_framework.parsers import FileUploadParser
from rest_framework.views import APIView

class FileUploadView(APIView):
    parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]
    
    def put(self, request, filename, format=None):
        file_obj = request.data['file']
        # ...
```

### How DRF gets the filename
DRF determines the filename using one of two methods:

1.  **URL keyword argument:** If the view is called with a `filename` URL keyword argument, that argument is used as the filename. This is typically configured in your `urls.py` using a regex pattern:
    `re_path(r'^upload/(?P<filename>[^/]+)$', FileUploadView.as_view())`
2.  **Content-Disposition header:** If no `filename` URL keyword argument is provided, the client must set the filename in the `Content-Disposition` HTTP header (e.g., `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=upload.jpg`).

llm_response:
Yes, you can combine permission rules using the `|` (or), `&` (and), and `~` (not) operators. You can also use brackets `()` to group expressions.

For your specific case of combining `IsAuthenticated` and a read-only rule, you can use the `|` operator within your `permission_classes` list:

```python
permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated | ReadOnly]
```

Alternatively, if you are looking for the built-in class that provides this specific functionality, you can use `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`, which allows authenticated users to perform any request and unauthenticated users to perform "safe" methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, or `OPTIONS`).

### AllowAny¶ {#allowany}

The
`AllowAny`
permission class will allow unrestricted access,
regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated
.

As with
`DjangoModelPermissions`
, this permission must only be applied to views that have a
`.queryset`
property or
`.get_queryset()`
method. Authorization will only be granted if the user
is authenticated
and has the
relevant per-object permissions
and
relevant model permissions

`POST`

`add`
permission on the model instance.
`PUT`
and
`PATCH`

permission on the model instance.

Note that
`DjangoObjectPermissions`
does not
require the
`django-guardian`
package, and should support other object-level backends equally well.

As with

you can use custom model permissions by overriding

and setting the

property.  Refer to the source code for details.

## Setting the permission policy¶ {#setting-the-permission-policy}

The default permission policy may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',]}`


If not specified, this setting defaults to allowing unrestricted access:


`'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny',]`


You can also set the authentication policy on a per-view, or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.


`fromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`


Or, if you're using the
`@api_view`
decorator with function based views.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to a subset of trusted administrators.

### IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly¶ {#isauthenticatedorreadonly}

The
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
will allow authenticated users to perform any request.  Requests for unauthenticated users will only be permitted if the request method is one of the "safe" methods;
`GET`
,
`HEAD`
or
`OPTIONS`
.

This permission is suitable if you want to your API to allow read permissions to anonymous users, and only allow write permissions to authenticated users.

### DjangoModelPermissions¶ {#djangomodelpermissions}

First add the following import in the views module


`fromrest_frameworkimportpermissions`


Then, add the following property to
both
the
`SnippetList`
and
`SnippetDetail`
view classes.


`permission_classes=[permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly]`


## Adding login to the Browsable API¶ {#adding-login-to-the-browsable-api}

If you open a browser and navigate to the browsable API at the moment, you'll find that you're no longer able to create new code snippets.  In order to do so we'd need to be able to login as a user.

We can add a login view for use with the browsable API, by editing the URLconf in our project-level
`urls.py`
file.

Add the following import at the top of the file:


`fromdjango.urlsimportpath,include`


And, at the end of the file, add a pattern to include the login and logout views for the browsable API.


`urlpatterns+=[path("api-auth/",include("rest_framework.urls")),]`


The
`'api-auth/'`
part of pattern can actually be whatever URL you want to use.

Permission checks are always run at the very start of the view, before any other code is allowed to proceed.  Permission checks will typically use the authentication information in the
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
properties to determine if the incoming request should be permitted.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

## How permissions are determined¶ {#how-permissions-are-determined}

Permissions in REST framework are always defined as a list of permission classes.

The default behavior can also be overridden to support custom model permissions.  For example, you might want to include a
`view`
model permission for
`GET`
requests.

To use custom model permissions, override
`DjangoModelPermissions`
and set the
`.perms_map`
property.  Refer to the source code for details.

### DjangoModelPermissionsOrAnonReadOnly¶ {#djangomodelpermissionsoranonreadonly}

Similar to
`DjangoModelPermissions`
, but also allows unauthenticated users to have read-only access to the API.

### DjangoObjectPermissions¶ {#djangoobjectpermissions}

This permission class ties into Django's standard
object permissions framework (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/auth/customizing/#handling-object-permissions)
that allows per-object permissions on models.  In order to use this permission class, you'll also need to add a permission backend that supports object-level permissions, such as
django-guardian (https://github.com/lukaszb/django-guardian)
.

To page through a huge, constantly-growing table efficiently without seeing duplicates when rows are inserted, you should use **`CursorPagination`** [4, 6].

*   **Ordering requirement:** It requires a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set [5]. By default, it orders by `"-created"`, which assumes the model has a `created` timestamp field [4].
*   **Complexity:** It is more complex than other pagination schemes [5].

# Pagination - Django REST framework

<https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/pagination>

# Pagination¶ {#pagination}

Django provides a few classes that help you manage paginated data – that is, data that’s split across several pages, with “Previous/Next” links.
—
Django documentation (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/pagination/)

REST framework includes support for customizable pagination styles. This allows you to modify how large result sets are split into individual pages of data.

The pagination API can support either:

Pagination links that are provided as part of the content of the response.
Pagination links that are included in response headers, such as
`Content-Range`
or
`Link`
.

The built-in styles currently all use links included as part of the content of the response. This style is more accessible when using the browsable API.

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly
`CursorPagination`
ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
Supports usage with very large datasets. With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable. Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail. You'll need to think about what ordering you want the scheme to be applied against. The default is to order by
`"-created"`
. This assumes that
there must be a 'created' timestamp field
on the model instances, and will present a "timeline" style paginated view, with the most recently added items first.

### CursorPagination¶ {#cursorpagination}

The cursor-based pagination presents an opaque "cursor" indicator that the client may use to page through the result set. This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.

Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Cursor based pagination is more complex than other schemes. It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. However it does provide the following benefits:

#### New pagination schemes.¶ {#new-pagination-schemes}

Until now, there has only been a single built-in pagination style in REST framework. We now have page, limit/offset and cursor based schemes included by default.

The cursor based pagination scheme is particularly smart, and is a better approach for clients iterating through large or frequently changing result sets. The scheme supports paging against non-unique indexes, by using both cursor and limit/offset information. It also allows for both forward and reverse cursor pagination. Much credit goes to David Cramer for
this blog post (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
on the subject.

#### Pagination controls in the browsable API.¶ {#pagination-controls-in-the-browsable-api}

Paginated results now include controls that render directly in the browsable API. If you're using the page or limit/offset style, then you'll see a page based control displayed in the browsable API:

The built-in styles currently all use links included as part of the content of the response. This style is more accessible when using the browsable API.

Pagination is only performed automatically if you're using the generic views or viewsets. If you're using a regular
`APIView`
, you'll need to call into the pagination API yourself to ensure you return a paginated response. See the source code for the
`mixins.ListModelMixin`
and
`generics.GenericAPIView`
classes for an example.

Pagination can be turned off by setting the pagination class to
`None`
.

## Setting the pagination style¶ {#setting-the-pagination-style}

The pagination style may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
and
`PAGE_SIZE`
setting keys. For example, to use the built-in limit/offset pagination, you would do something like this:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`

reference: Apply a UniqueTogetherValidator in the serializer's Meta.validators with the queryset and the field names that must be unique as a set; note it implicitly treats those fields as required.

llm_response:
To prevent a user from creating two records with the same combination of two fields, you should use the `UniqueTogetherValidator`.

This validator is applied to the `Meta` class of your serializer. You must provide the `queryset` to be validated against and a list of the `fields` that must form a unique set.

Example usage:

```python
from rest_framework.validators import UniqueTogetherValidator

class ExampleSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    # ...
    class Meta:
        validators = [
            UniqueTogetherValidator(
                queryset=ToDoItem.objects.all(),
                fields=['list', 'position']
            )
        ]
```

**Important considerations:**
*   **Required Fields:** The `UniqueTogetherValidator` implicitly treats all fields it applies to as `required=True`, unless they have a `default` value.
*   **Read-Only Fields:** If a field involved in a `unique_together` constraint is read-only (e.g., a user field), you must explicitly declare the field on the serializer with both `read_only=True` and a `default` value (such as `serializers.CurrentUserDefault()`) to ensure the validator can still function.
*   **Ambiguity:** If you need to set one of the fields to `required=False`, the validation behavior becomes ambiguous, and you may need to handle the validation explicitly.

There are some ambiguous cases where you'll need to instead handle validation
explicitly, rather than relying on the default serializer classes that
`ModelSerializer`
generates.

reference: APIClient, which extends Django's test Client and supports the same .get()/.post()/.put()/.patch()/.delete()/.head()/.options() interface.
